knowledge_point.title: Finding the Derivative of a Parametric Curve

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186083240/plots/d7f3b05ffc420dbca0eff6.png)

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=6\left(2t{e}^{t}\right),\,y=4\left({t}^{2}+2t\right),\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6\left(2{e}^{t}(t+1)\right),\,{y}^{′}(t)=4\left(2t+2\right).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4\left(2t+2\right)}{6\left(2{e}^{t}(t+1)\right)}=\frac{4\left(1\right)}{6\left({e}^{t}\right)}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{4\left(1\right)}{6\left({e}^{1}\right)} \\  & =\frac{4\left(1\right)}{6\left(e\right)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

derivative_domain.condition: x'(t) and y'(t) exist and x'(t) != 0

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=4\left(5\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\right),\,y=4\left(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\right),\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Give an exact answer.

$\frac{dy}{dx}{|}_{t\,=\,\pi /6}=$ 
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\left(10\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\right),\,{y}^{′}(t)=4\left(-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\right).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4\left((-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\right)}{4\left(10\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\right)}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

derivative_domain.condition: x'(t) and y'(t) exist and x'(t) != 0

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=6\left({e}^{2t}\right),\,y=5\left(({t}^{2}-1){e}^{-t}\right),\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6\left(2{e}^{2t}\right),\,{y}^{′}(t)=5\left((1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-t}\right).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5\left((1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-t}\right)}{6\left(2{e}^{2t}\right)}=\frac{5\left(1\right)}{6\left(2\right)}(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-3t}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{5\left(1\right)}{6\left(2\right)}(1+2(1)-(1)^{2}){e}^{-3(1)} \\  & =\frac{5\left(1\right)}{6\left(2\right)}(1+2-1){e}^{-3} \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\left({e}^{-3}\right)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
